Gastroenterology · published research

Colon anastomoses

Summary of the Evidence

Three publications from one Spanish research group examined 633-nm helium-neon laser after rat colon anastomosis. Two early reports assessed mechanical and histologic healing after 3.6 J/cm², while a later high-risk experiment compared repeated 1.9- and 6.4-J/cm² exposure. They are related publications from one group, not independent replications. No human study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

No clinical trial has shown that PBM reduces anastomotic leakage, infection, reoperation, or recovery time after human colorectal surgery. Bursting strength in rats is relevant to mechanical integrity but is not equivalent to clinical leak rates.

Animal evidence

The 1988 report found higher bursting pressure and wall tension at postoperative days 2, 4, and 7 without the luminal narrowing seen in controls. A related histology report described more fibroblasts and round cells in scar tissue, new-vessel formation, and epithelialization after two 3.6-J/cm² exposures (Asencio-Arana et al. 1988; Asencio-Arana et al. 1990).

In the high-risk model, repeated 1.9-J/cm² exposure nearly doubled day-4 bursting strength. The 6.4-J/cm² protocol did not show the same benefit, and hydroxyproline differences were not statistically significant. This indicates a protocol-specific response rather than greater benefit from a higher dose (Asencio-Arana et al. 1992).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The studies used approximately 633-nm red helium-neon laser light. Reported fluences were 3.6 J/cm² in the early healing work and 1.9 versus 6.4 J/cm² in the high-risk model. Treatment was local or endoscopic and outcomes were assessed over days. The experiments did not compare modern devices or establish an optimal schedule, and rat tissue depth, surgery, and recovery differ from human postoperative care.

Interpretation

Selected low-fluence protocols improved early mechanical or histologic healing in rats, while the higher tested fluence did not reproduce the strength effect. The evidence is old, comes from one group, and does not show that PBM prevents anastomotic leaks in patients. Independent animal replication followed by clinical studies would be needed before drawing a clinical conclusion.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)Very low for early anastomotic strength and healing measures in rats

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Three related publications from one Spanish group report stronger early rat-colon anastomoses or favorable histology after selected 633-nm helium-neon laser protocols. The high-risk experiment found benefit at 1.9 J/cm² but not 6.4 J/cm². The evidence is old, preclinical, and lacks independent replication or human leakage outcomes, so certainty remains very low.
